analysis.one_liner: Eliminates tuition at community colleges and for working- and middle-class students at public four-year colleges.
analysis.headline: The bill has been referred to three House committees since its introduction in May 2025, with no hearing, markup, or vote, and 75 of 217 House Democrats have signed on as cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a federal-state partnership that pays states to eliminate tuition and required fees for every student at community colleges and for working- and middle-class students at public four-year colleges, with income cutoffs of $150,000 for single households and $300,000 for married households. It would roughly double the maximum Pell Grant to $14,790 at public and tribal colleges, let students use it for living expenses, extend how long it can be used, and open it to Dreamer students. It would also fund tuition elimination at private nonprofit historically Black colleges and minority-serving institutions and reauthorize TRIO and GEAR UP college-access programs.
analysis.who_benefits: Every student at a public community college or two-year tribal college, regardless of income, would have tuition and fees fully eliminated. Students from families making up to $150,000 (single) or $300,000 (married couples) would get free tuition at public four-year colleges. Pell Grant recipients would see the maximum award rise to $14,790 at public and tribal institutions, could use it for living costs, and would have more years to use it. Dreamer students and students with other immigration statuses would become eligible for federal aid. Students at private nonprofit historically Black colleges and minority-serving institutions would also get free tuition.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Community college students and middle-income families

how_it_helps.text: Provides federal grants covering 100% of the cost of eliminating tuition and fees for all students at community colleges and two-year tribal colleges, declining to 80% federal funding by 2031, with states picking up the rest.

Eliminates tuition and fees at public four-year colleges for working- and middle-class students, defined as dependent students from single-parent households making up to $150,000 or married-parent households up to $300,000, with the same limits for independent students.

Raises the maximum Pell Grant to $14,790 at public and tribal institutions, extends the time limit to seven and a half years, allows use for living and nontuition expenses, and makes Dreamer students eligible.
Funds tuition elimination at private nonprofit historically Black colleges and universities and minority-serving institutions, and caps how fast those institutions can raise tuition.

Requires participating states to keep instruction spending and state higher education funding at or above recent-year levels, to move toward 75% of instruction being taught by tenured or tenure-track faculty, and to make community college credits fully transferable to four-year programs.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government pays the largest share through direct appropriations with no tax increases or spending offsets in the bill text, so the cost falls on federal taxpayers and the deficit. States must contribute a share that grows from 0% to 20% by 2031 and must maintain higher education funding at recent-year levels, so state taxpayers bear part of the cost. Students in states that choose not to participate get nothing.

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates 'such sums as may be necessary' for fiscal years 2026 through 2035 directly out of the Treasury, with no revenue source, tax, or spending offset anywhere in the bill text, so the entire cost would be added to federal deficits unless separate legislation pays for it.

The income cutoffs for free tuition at four-year schools are generous: a married couple earning up to $300,000 a year would qualify, which is several times the national median household income, so a substantial share of the benefit goes to families well above the middle.

The benefit depends on states opting in: a state that refuses to pay its growing share or meet maintenance-of-effort requirements gets no grant, so students in non-participating states would see no change.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to students is large and concrete: a tuition-free path through community college for everyone and free public four-year tuition for most middle-income families, plus a doubled Pell Grant for the lowest-income students. The honest objection is the bill's design as an open-ended entitlement: it appropriates unlimited mandatory sums with no way to pay for them, which means either larger deficits or a future fight over funding. The $300,000 married-household cutoff also spreads benefits well up the income scale rather than concentrating them on families who most need help. The federal-state structure protects against states cutting their own higher education budgets to grab federal money, which is a genuine strength.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced and has had no hearing, markup, or floor action since.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the College for All Act of 2025 in the House on May 21, 2025, with 27 original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the Education and Workforce Committee and additionally to the Ways and Means and Budget Committees.
75 House Democrats have signed on as cosponsors, all from one party.
The action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action after the initial referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has clearly won or lost yet, since the Congress is still in session and the bill could in theory still move. As of now the status quo holds: students continue paying tuition at public colleges, and for-profit colleges, student lenders, and other private colleges are unaffected by anything the bill would do. With no Republican support and no committee action, the bill is on the usual path to expiring without a vote at the end of the Congress, which would leave tuition-paying students and institutions relying on tuition revenue in the same position as before it was introduced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill sits in committee

sides.party_line_note: All 75 cosponsors are Democrats, no Republican has signed on, and the bill sits in committees controlled by the Republican House majority, which has scheduled no action on it.

industries.note: The bill excludes proprietary (for-profit) institutions from receiving any state fiscal support and bars institutions that converted from for-profit to nonprofit status from the tuition-free grant program for 25 years, while free public college would pull away their potential students. For-profit colleges historically enroll students with federal aid and charge more than public alternatives, so their loss corresponds to a public gain.

With tuition and fees fully eliminated for participants and Pell Grants usable for living expenses, students would need to borrow far less. The bill also prohibits participants from applying financial aid toward tuition, so lenders' main market shrinks in every participating state.

industries.industry: Private nonprofit colleges (other than HBCUs and minority-serving institutions)
industries.note: These schools are not eligible for the tuition-free grants, and free public options would draw students away from institutions that rely on tuition revenue. However, if they compete for the same students, some pressure toward lower prices could follow.

industries.industry: Private nonprofit historically Black colleges and minority-serving institutions
industries.note: They receive federal grants to eliminate tuition and fees for eligible students, with limits on how fast they can raise tuition. Students at these institutions get free tuition without paying higher fees elsewhere.

Public institutions become the permanent channel for a large federal benefit: the bill locks in their role as the tuition-free option and requires states to maintain per-student funding, instruction spending, and tenure-track faculty hiring to keep receiving grants. Students get free tuition, and the institutions get protected, guaranteed funding.

Participating states must commit to having 75% of instruction delivered by tenured or tenure-track faculty within five years and to prioritize hiring from the existing contingent pool for those positions, and part-time faculty must be paid for out-of-classroom work like office hours.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has sat in three committees since May 2025 with no hearing or markup, and with no Republican cosponsors it is very unlikely to advance in a House controlled by the other party. The most probable path is expiring at the end of the 119th Congress without a vote, unless its funding framework is attached to a larger bill that can pass under the majority's control.
